newsitem.title: JAPAN: US auto group knocks Japan for not opening market.
newsitem.headline: US auto group knocks Japan for not opening market.

text.p: The head of an influential U.S. auto manufacturers group on Thursday lashed out at Japan for what he said was the country's slow progress in opening up its automobile market, evident in its growing trade surplus.

"I don't criticise Japanese carmakers. I am criticising the lack of progress in opening the Japanese market and the growing trade surplus between the United States and Japan," Andrew Card, the president and CEO of the American Automobile Manufacturers Association (AAMA), told reporters during his visit in Tokyo.

"Figures released just this morning here in Tokyo showed that Japan's surplus with the U.S. and EU increased 100 percent in the first half of 1997. The surplus with U.S. alone is up 48 percent. These numbers are reaching a politically unsustainable level," Card said.
Japan's Finance Ministry said on Thursday that the country's customs-cleared trade surplus in the first half of 1997 rose 28.4 percent from a year earlier to 3.98 trillion yen ($34.3 billion).
Japan's trade surplus with the United States jumped 48.8 percent and with the European Union 43.9 percent in the first six months of this year compared with the same period a year earlier, it said.
Card said that the excessively weak yen against the dollar had created great export opportunities for Japanese automakers.
"This (Japanese) market is not opened. The U.S. market is. There are many many Japanese makers taking advantage of the opened U.S. market," Card said.
Card said that only 12 agreements to open new dealer outlets for U.S. car companies have been signed since last November.

And the number of new dealer outlets which signed franchise agreements with General Motors Corp, Ford Motor Co or Chrysler Corp since the 1995 Japan-U.S. auto agreement totalled 126, far below the 200 outlets the U.S. government and carmakers had expected by the end of 1996, Card said.

"They (U.S. officials) are very, very sensitive to the auto sector relationship between the United States and Japan," Card said. "I know there will be political traction if the trade relationship keeps heading the direction that it is heading right now," Card said.

He said U.S. car sales in Japan fell 13.6 percent in the first half of 1997, adding that Japan has a special responsibility in setting an example for the world's trading partners by actively promoting a fully free and open marketplace in Japan.
Japanese industry data showed that genuine foreign cars -- excluding those made by Japanese automakers overseas -- rose 1.6 percent from a year earlier to 166,932.

In terms of restrictions that could stifle imports, Japan does not impose an import tax on cars and trucks but the United States has a 2.5 percent tax on imported cars and 25 percent tax on imported trucks.

Fears of a possible flare-up in trade friction have been in the headlines recently, exacerbated by U.S. President Bill Clinton's comments at last month's summit of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations that Japan would risk an economic war with the United States if its trade surplus started exploding again.

A Japanese Finance Ministry official on Thursday attributed a decline in purchases of imports such as cars and clothing on the increase in the national consumption tax from three percent to five percent in April.
